# Fall River/New Bedford Line
The Fall River/New Bedford Line (formerly the Middleborough/Lakeville Line) is a commuter rail line of the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) serving southeastern Massachusetts in the United States. It runs from Boston’s South Station through the South Shore region to a junction at East Taunton, then splits into two branches terminating in the cities of Fall River and New Bedford. The line was extended and renamed in March 2025 as part of the South Coast Rail project, restoring passenger train service to Fall River and New Bedford for the first time since 1958. The 2025 extension added six new stations and about 37 miles of track to the MBTA commuter rail network. The project cost approximately $1.1 billion and had been in planning for decades, with initial projections in the 1990s targeting a 1997 opening. Trains on the line take roughly 90 to 95 minutes to travel between South Station and either Fall River or New Bedford. The Fall River/New Bedford Line operates in MBTA fare Zone 8 (the outermost zone), with a one-way full fare of $12.25 (or $6 for reduced-fare passengers) as of 2025.
## Route and Service
Map of the Fall River/New Bedford Line route. The line shares its initial route with other Old Colony Lines, beginning at South Station in Boston and running south through Quincy and Braintree. It then continues along the former Old Colony Railroad mainline through Brockton and Bridgewater to Middleborough. A new Middleborough station was constructed slightly north of the old Middleborough/Lakeville stop, to enable the connection toward Fall River and New Bedford. At East Taunton, the route branches: one Fall River branch heads southwest through Freetown to the Fall River Depot terminal, and the New Bedford branch runs south through a Church Street stop into downtown New Bedford, where it terminates at New Bedford station. These were all newly built stations opened with the 2025 project, in addition to East Taunton and the relocated Middleborough station, totaling six new stations. The existing stations between Boston and Middleborough (such as Braintree, Brockton, and Bridgewater) remained part of the line. Fall River, New Bedford, and Taunton had been the largest Massachusetts cities within 50 miles of Boston without commuter rail service until this extension was completed.
MBTA commuter trains on the Fall River/New Bedford Line provide a “one-seat” ride from the South Coast region to Boston. On weekdays, a full schedule of direct trains serves both branches: typically 15 inbound/outbound trips per day on the Fall River side and 17 on the New Bedford side. In total, 32 daily trains run between South Station and the East Taunton junction on weekdays, with trains generally operating about every 70 minutes during commuter hours. On weekends, service is less frequent (about every two hours), with a combined 26 trips per day between Boston and East Taunton and alternating service to each branch. The final departures each night leave South Station around midnight to reach New Bedford and Fall River in the late night hours. In addition to the direct Boston trains, some shuttle train trips are scheduled between East Taunton and the branch endpoints to augment service frequency; East Taunton station functions as a transfer point in certain off-peak times. All trains on the line are diesel-operated, as the route is not electrified (consistent with the rest of the MBTA’s Old Colony commuter lines). The line’s new stations offer parking facilities, and initial promotions included free parking and free fares at the new South Coast stations for a limited time after opening.
Early ridership figures have shown a significant increase in usage after the line’s launch. By mid-2025, the MBTA was recording roughly 2,000 more daily passenger trips on the Fall River/New Bedford corridor compared to the previous year, when the service only ran to Middleborough/Lakeville. This represents about a 33% rise in ridership along the line, at a time when overall MBTA commuter rail ridership was slightly declining. Weekday commuter trips accounted for most of the surge (over one-third higher than before), indicating strong demand from South Coast residents traveling to jobs in the Boston area. Local officials have welcomed the new service as a means to improve regional connectivity and economic opportunity, though transportation analysts note that a shift from highways to rail will take time; highway traffic data in late 2025 did not yet show a noticeable decrease in car volumes on routes from the South Coast to Boston.
## History and Development
Regular passenger rail service to New Bedford, Fall River, and Taunton was discontinued in the late 1950s, when the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad ended its Old Colony Division commuter operations due to financial losses. The last train from New Bedford ran in September 1958, marking the end of an era in which those cities had been connected to Boston by rail for about a century. In the decades that followed, southeastern Massachusetts became the only major region around Greater Boston without commuter rail access. State transportation officials periodically studied restoring service, and by the late 1980s the MBTA had initial plans to extend the Stoughton Line through Taunton as a direct route to the South Coast. In 1991, Governor William Weld publicly committed to have commuter rail running to Fall River and New Bedford by 1997, and some state bond funding was authorized for the project in the mid-1990s. Preliminary work even began in 1998, when a groundbreaking was held and bridge upgrades started, despite the route not being finalized at the time. However, the ambitious schedule proved untenable. In 2003, the plan was halted by Governor Mitt Romney, citing budget constraints and the MBTA’s inability to finance new expansions at that time. This pause left the South Coast Rail initiative stalled for several years.
The project regained momentum in the late 2000s. In 2007, Governor Deval Patrick’s administration re-launched the South Coast Rail planning process, affirming it as a priority for the state and estimating the cost at $1.4 billion. Over the next several years, detailed environmental reviews and engineering plans were developed. By 2014, the Massachusetts legislature had authorized $2.3 billion in capital funding for the project as cost projections grew. A major decision came in 2017, when the MBTA and MassDOT elected to pursue the South Coast Rail in two phases. Phase I would use the existing Middleborough/Lakeville Line right-of-way to provide service to New Bedford and Fall River more quickly, while Phase II would later build a more direct route (via the previously planned Stoughton Line extension) in the future. The two-phase approach was somewhat controversial locally—some officials in New Bedford were skeptical of the indirect Phase I route—but it allowed construction to begin sooner on the available rights-of-way. Under the Phase I plan, trains from Boston would travel the longer Old Colony route via Middleborough, and a new connection from Middleborough to East Taunton would link to the South Coast branches. Phase II (the “Full Build”) was envisioned to follow in the 2030s, providing a straighter path from Boston through Stoughton and Taunton with electrified tracks and additional stations, reducing travel times by 15–25 minutes.
Construction of Phase I officially broke ground in mid-2019 after the necessary permits and funding were in place. Early action work included upgrading existing freight lines, replacing track, and building new bridges to handle passenger service. By late 2022, as the project neared completion, voters in New Bedford and Fall River overwhelmingly approved joining the MBTA service district in their communities. This local referendum was required to integrate the cities into the MBTA network and commit to the associated local funding formula. The physical construction of tracks, signals, and stations for Phase I was largely finished by the end of 2023. Testing and crew training took several additional months, and the start of service, originally hoped for late 2023, was postponed slightly into the next year. The Fall River/New Bedford Line officially opened for passenger service on March 24, 2025. Opening ceremonies were held at the new stations, and the inaugural trains from New Bedford (departing at 4:27 a.m.) and Fall River (5:05 a.m.) carried enthusiastic first-day riders including local officials. The MBTA offered free rides during the first week of operations and on all weekends in April 2025 to encourage the public to try the new service. It had been roughly 65 years since residents of the South Coast cities last had passenger rail, a milestone noted by officials at the launch.
In the months following the launch, some operational challenges emerged. The MBTA had to adjust schedules by mid-2025 to improve reliability and address community feedback. In July 2025, the agency modified the timetable by shifting some departure times and eliminating two late-night shuttle trains that had been running from East Taunton to the branch termini after midnight. These changes were made to reduce noise disturbances in residential areas near the tracks and to improve on-time performance. Despite early hiccups such as a period of crew shortages causing a few train cancellations in April 2025, the line’s performance stabilized, and by mid-year the MBTA reported more consistent operations on the new service.
## Future Plans
The Fall River/New Bedford Line as opened in 2025 represents the first phase of South Coast Rail, and planning continues for further improvements. Phase II of the project (the “Full Build”) will create a more direct rail corridor from Boston to the South Coast by extending the MBTA Stoughton Branch south through Easton and Taunton to connect with the Phase I route at East Taunton. This full build would include several additional stations (for example, a station in downtown Taunton is anticipated, among others along the new route) and would shorten the travel distance to Fall River and New Bedford. It is also mandated to be an electrified line, as required by a state law for the Stoughton extension. Phase II is not yet funded and, as of 2025, has no firm timeline for construction; MBTA officials have indicated it will not open until the 2030s at the earliest. The realization of Phase II will depend on future capital funding and the resolution of environmental permitting challenges (the Stoughton route passes through sensitive wetlands that were a source of delay in the past).
There are also proposals to extend commuter rail service beyond the current termini. One active idea is to further extend the Middleborough branch southward to reach Buzzards Bay on Cape Cod. The CapeFlyer seasonal train already uses the Cape Cod rail line in summer, but local lawmakers have suggested making year-round service to the Buzzards Bay area a part of the MBTA system. In 2023 a bill was introduced in the state legislature to require the MBTA to run commuter trains from Middleborough (Lakeville) to Buzzards Bay with several daily trips, as a first step toward eventually serving other Cape Cod towns. This proposal remains under study and would require additional agreements (such as track upgrades and coordination with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for the Cape Cod Canal railroad bridge). If pursued, a Buzzards Bay extension could potentially be operated as an offshoot of the Fall River/New Bedford Line, since it would branch from the same vicinity near Middleborough. As of late 2025, no funding has been allocated for this expansion, but local interest in better rail connections to Cape Cod continues to be voiced.

MBTA launches South Coast Rail service (updated)
================================================

[By Trains Staff](https://www.trains.com/author/trainsstaff/) | March 24, 2025| Last updated on August 6, 2025

 [![Image 12: Facebook Logo](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/themes/understrap-child/images/social/social_facebook.png)](javascript:void\(0\))[![Image 13: X Twitter Logo](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/themes/understrap-child/images/social/social_x.png)](javascript:void\(0\))[![Image 14: Reddit Logo](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/themes/understrap-child/images/social/social_reddit.png)](javascript:void\(0\))[![Image 15: Linkedin Logo](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/themes/understrap-child/images/social/social_linkedIn.png)](javascript:void\(0\))[![Image 16: Email Logo](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/themes/understrap-child/images/social/social_email.png)](javascript:void\(0\))

  

**Addition brings commuter rail to three largest cities within 50 miles of Boston not previously served**

### Email Newsletter

Get the newest photos, videos, stories, and more from Trains.com brands. Sign-up for email today!

 

Get Updates

![Image 17: People standing on platform waiting to board commuter train](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/TRN_South_Coast_Rail_starts.jpg)

Passengers wait to board the MBTA’s first South Coast Rail train in New Bedford, Mass., in a s screenshot from [a WBZ-TV video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M9BId-h53d8).

* * *

BOSTON — Massachusetts’ South Coast Rail commuter operation is now officially in service.

[The 37-mile addition](https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail) to the MBTA commuter rail network launched today (March 24, 2025), with the [_Fall River Herald News_ reporting](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/24/mbta-south-coast-rail-to-fall-river-new-bedford-starts-rolling/82627178007/) that well over 100 people were on hand to catch the first train, a  scheduled 4:27 a.m. departure from New Bedford. That is one of  the six stations on the two-branch addition. The first train from Fall River, endpoint of the other branch, also drew a crowd for its 5:05 a.m. departure, including Mayor Paul Coogan and state Rep. Carole Fiola.

![Image 18: Map of MBTA commuter rail line between Boston and Fall River/New Bedford, Mass.](https://www.trains.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/TRN_MBTA_South_Coast_Rail.jpg)

The MBTA’s South Coast Rail extension is in service as of March 24, 2025. MBTA

Other new stations are at Church Street on the New Bedford branch and Freetown on the Fall River route; the two come together at East Taunton. The final new station is at Middleborough, where the new route joins the existing Middleborough/Lakeville line. With the opening of the extension, that route is now known as the Fall River/New Bedford Line. Fall River, New Bedord, and Tauton had been the three largest communities within 50 miles of Boston without commuter rail service.

The extension, which cost approximately $1.1 billion, at one time was projected to open in 1997.

“After years of delays, we took this challenge head on and delivered for the people of the South Coast — and our entire state will benefit,” Gov. Maura Healey said in [an event at the East Taunton station](https://www.mbta.com/news/2025-03-24/healey-driscoll-administration-massdot-mbta-celebrate-launch-south-coast-rail?utm_term=commuter-rail&utm_campaign=curated-content&utm_content=Healey-Driscoll+Administration%2C+MassDOT%2C+MBTA+Celebrate+Launch+of+South+Coast+Rail&utm_medium=news&utm_source=homepage) marking the start of service. “The start of rail service will give people more options for how to get around, where to live and where to work. It means less traffic congestion and shorter commutes, giving people more time back with their loved ones.”

Said MBTA CEO Phillip Eng, “This is truly a day for celebration for all, in particular for the many stakeholders who long advocated for this service. It is through the collaboration of an incredible number of MBTA teams, contractor crews, our MassDOT partners, many community members, elected officials, our operating partners at Keolis, and so many more. I am so grateful for their dedication and tremendous hard work. Today, we make history together and welcome back our southeastern Mass. passengers to the T.”  It had been 65 years since the South Coast communities had rail passenger service.

Trips between Boston’s South Station and either endpoint will take about 90 minutes; eventually, a full-fare ticket will be $12.25 from all six of the new stations, with reduced fares of $6 [available for qualified riders](https://www.mbta.com/fares/reduced). However, officials announced last week that all travel to or from the new stations will be free through March 31; after that, free travel will continue on weekends through the end of April \[see [“MBTA expands free service …,”](https://www.trains.com/trn/news-reviews/news-wire/mbta-expands-free-service-for-launch-of-south-coast-rail/) _Trains_ News Wire, March 21, 2025\]. Parking will also be free at the new stations through the end of April, subject to availability.

The service that launched today is actually Phase 1 of a project envisioned to eventually provide a more direct route to Fall River and New Bedford by extending the MBTA’s current Stoughton Line to connect with the new service at its East Taunton station, That extension, called the Full Build by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, would also lead to four additional stations, but is currently unfunded and has no timeline for construction.

_— Updated at 9:30 p.m. CT with comments from press conference to mark the start of service._

The “Full Build” version of South Coast Rail would provide a more direct route by extending the current Stoughton Line. MassDOT

The MBTA announced Friday that its South Coast Rail would begin passenger service next month, extending commuter rail access to Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro, and Fall River for the first time in 65 years.

##### South Coast Rail:

*   [![Image 4](https://bdc2020.o0bc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/55T4HGVFRDCBG2H4PHUP6B66MA-666f96c9963b9-768x432.jpg) #### South Coast commuter rail extension start delayed again to spring 2025](https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2024/06/16/south-coast-commuter-rail-extension-start-delayed-again-to-spring-2025/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feature)
*   [#### The South Coast Rail is on track. What could it mean for housing?](https://www.boston.com/real-estate/spring-house-hunt/2024/04/10/south-coast-rail-on-track-what-mean-housing/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feed)

Passenger service, which kicks off March 24, was initially slated to begin in late 2023 when the project broke ground in 2019, but has been [repeatedly delayed](https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2024/06/16/south-coast-commuter-rail-extension-start-delayed-again-to-spring-2025/).

Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford are the only major cities within 50 miles of Boston that do not currently have access to Boston on the commuter rail, and when the South Coast Rail opens in March, it will connect southeastern Massachusetts residents to Boston in a “one-seat trip” for the first time since the late 1950s.

Advertisement:

To create the South Coast Rail, the MBTA extended the existing Middleborough/Lakeville Line, which will be renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line.

The MBTA said there will be 15 trips on the Fall River Line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line each day, for a total of 32 trips between South Station and East Taunton daily. It estimated trains will run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every two hours on weekends, when there will be a total of 26 trips between South Station and East Taunton. The last trains will leave just before midnight.

“The people of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro and Fall River have been waiting for passenger rail service for far too long,” said Governor Maura Healey in a statement.

Advertisement:

She said the rail will “reduce congestion and spur economic development.”

Fares for all South Coast Rail stations will be priced in Zone 8, a full fare of $12.25 and a reduced fare of $6.

As part of the commuter rail’s “all day service model,” shuttles will also run between each terminus point and East Taunton Station, allowing for more frequent service.

“We continue to improve mass transportation across our networks to make it the preferred choice of travel,” said MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng in a statement. “Delivering new rail service to the communities as part of South Coast Rail is another example of our workforce fulfilling commitments made to the public.”

On March 24, 2025, the Middleborough/Lakeville Line extended to Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, and Fall River, expanding Commuter Rail service between southeastern Massachusetts and Boston! The line has been renamed to the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/).

The [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/) offers six newly constructed and accessible stations, connecting communities between Boston and the South Coast of Massachusetts. Skip the traffic, save time and money, and try taking the Fall River/New Bedford Line!

Free Fares at New Stations Every Weekend through May
----------------------------------------------------

**To celebrate the new Fall River/New Bedford Line, the Commuter Rail will offer free weekend service.**

For every weekend (Saturdays and Sundays) between April 5 to May 31, on April 21 (Patriots’ Day) and May 26 (Memorial Day), the Fall River/New Bedford Line will offer fare-free service. Passengers can ride for free if they board or end their ride at one of the six new stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line. This offer is valid for on-board purchases. Please speak with the conductor about your origin and destination stations. This offer only applies for those on the Fall River and New Bedford Commuter Rail Lines and does not apply to trains on other Commuter Rail Lines. Weekdays operate as regular Commuter Rail fares.

Parking is also free at six of the Fall River/New Bedford Line station lots from March 24 until the end of day on April 30, 2025:

*   [Middleborough](https://massbytrain.com/stations/middleborough/)
*   [East Taunton](https://massbytrain.com/stations/east-taunton/)
*   [Freetown](https://massbytrain.com/stations/freetown/)
*   [Church Street](https://massbytrain.com/stations/church-street/)
*   [Fall River Depot](https://massbytrain.com/stations/fall-river-depot/)
*   [New Bedford](https://massbytrain.com/stations/new-bedford/)

_\*Note: This free parking promotion might end earlier if Fall River/New Bedford Line parking lots fill up and spaces become unavailable. The standard parking rates for these stations are $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays._

![Image 1: Map of the Fall River/New Bedford Line on the Commuter Rail](https://massbytrain.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map-181x300.png)

Fall River/New Bedford Line Service Schedules
---------------------------------------------

There are 15 weekday trips on the Fall River Line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line. On weekends, the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) operates 26 trips between [South Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/south-station/) and East Taunton. Trains run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every 2 hours on the weekends. The Fall River/New Bedford Line also offers late-night service, with the last train departing Boston around midnight.

In addition to direct service, [East Taunton Station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NBM-0374) serves as a transfer station; additional trains operate between East Taunton and the Fall River and New Bedford branches, offering connections between Boston and both the Fall River and New Bedford branches on most trips.

Changes with the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line
----------------------------------------------------------

For regular Commuter Rail passengers, there are a number of changes to take note of:

*   The Middleborough/Lakeville Line is now called the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
*   The Middleborough/Lakeville Station is now called [Middleborough Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/middleborough/) and is located at 52 West Grove Street, Middleborough, MA 02346. The former Middleborough/Lakeville station located at 125 Commercial Drive, Lakeville is now Lakeville Station and only serves [CapeFLYER](https://massbytrain.com/special-service/capeflyer/) service.

Fares
-----

Commuter rail ridership in southeast Massachusetts has surged since South Coast Rail service began in March. On average, riders are taking 2,000 more trips each day on the MBTA’s Fall River/New Bedford line than they did last year, when the route was the Middleborough/Lakeville line. The new trips amount to a 33% increase in ridership along the line, even as ridership across the MBTA commuter rail network overall decreased by 6%. “I think it’s awesome,” said Seth Kaplan, a transit advocate with the Boston-based group [TransitMatters](https://transitmatters.org/). “There’s a demand there for people who once had transit to have it restored to them.” The Light’s analysis was based on MBTA ridership data from April through September 2025, compared to the same period in 2024. If the 2,000 new daily trips are coming mainly from South Coast riders, that would exceed [previous estimates](https://www.mass.gov/files/documents/2018/08/10/SCR_DSEIR_ExecSummary.pdf) that the extension would generate 1,600 new daily trips. “We want ridership to be as high as possible, given the investment the state made in this infrastructure,” said Chris Dempsey, a transit advocate who served as the state’s assistant secretary of transportation under Gov. Deval Patrick. “2,000 per day is a respectable and encouraging number.” ![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/ridership-stats.png?resize=780%2C623&ssl=1) The long-awaited [South Coast Rail](https://newbedfordlight.org/southcoastrail) extension [added](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/) six new stations to the MBTA network, bringing passenger rail back to the region for the first time [since 1958](https://newbedfordlight.org/key-points-on-the-route-to-south-coast-rail-2/). Local leaders [celebrated](https://newbedfordlight.org/gov-healey-mayor-vips-celebrate-opening-of-south-coast-rail/) the extension as a way to connect residents to better jobs and schools to the north, as well as another way to attract tourists to the South Coast. The latest ridership data offers some insight into how riders are using the service. ### **Who’s taking the T?** Local museum and business owners told The Light this spring that they saw an [uptick](https://newbedfordlight.org/new-bedfords-on-track-for-bump-in-visitors-this-year/) in Bostonian visitors. But the data suggests that commuting workers, rather than leisure travelers, make up most of the increased ridership. Weekday ridership increased by 36%, while weekend ridership increased by only 13%. Ridership on Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Labor Day — federal holidays when many workers have the day off — looked more like what you’d see on a typical weekend day. Even as peak tourism season ended, ridership remained at roughly the same levels through the fall. The recent data only shows ridership on the Fall River/New Bedford Line as a whole. It doesn’t show exactly how many people were going to or from the new South Coast stations. ### **Is it helping traffic?** At the South Coast Rail kickoff celebration on March 24, Gov. Maura Healey [touted](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HKYzdq9ISFc) the project’s benefits for drivers. * * * ### [Local news needs your support before the year ends ⇢](https://newbedfordlight.org/support-our-publication/) * * * “It’s gonna help with traffic congestion, which is something that we’ve made a priority,” she said. “We want shorter commute times for both train riders and car drivers.” A [state environmental analysis](https://www.mass.gov/doc/south-coast-rail-dseir-executive-summary/download) from 2017 predicted that the project would shift some commutes from roads to rails, resulting in a reduction of 66,400 “vehicle miles traveled” each day. That’s equivalent to eliminating roughly 600 daily round-trip commutes between New Bedford and Boston. But there’s no sign that the trains have taken a significant number of cars off the roads between the South Coast and Boston, according to The Light’s analysis of state traffic data. Freeway traffic on Route 24 and Route 140 is about the same as last year. That didn’t surprise transit advocates. “The reality is, as much as we wish transit service would solve congestion, that alone is not sufficient,” said Dempsey, the former Patrick administration official. ![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/whalestooth.png?resize=780%2C439&ssl=1) The long-awaited South Coast Rail extension [added](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/) six new stations to the MBTA network, bringing passenger rail back to the region for the first time since 1958. Credit: Grace Ferguson / The New Bedford Light * * * Get local news delivered straight to your inbox. ------------------------------------------------ * Daily Newsletter A dose of New Bedford news in your inbox each weekday morning * The Weekender Catch up on the week’s biggest stories every Saturday morning Sign up * * * The promises of less traffic on Route 24 may have been “overstated,” Dempsey said. He noted a concept in transportation called “induced demand” — when the government tries to relieve congestion by building a new road or train line, this can actually encourage more people to travel, resulting in more traffic and the same amount of congestion. The traffic data isn’t perfect. A spokesperson for the Massachusetts Department of Transportation cautioned that [traffic counts](https://mhd.public.ms2soft.com/tcds/tsearch.asp?loc=Mhd&mod=TCDS) along this corridor are limited, and any findings from those counts would be “inconclusive.” With that in mind, here’s what the data shows. A traffic counter on Route 24, just south of the Harrison Boulevard exit in Avon, logged a slight increase in traffic during the past several months, compared to the same time last year. The average number of cars passing the counter each day between April and October increased 2% from 2024 to 2025. Another traffic counter on Route 140 in Freetown showed a 1% increase in traffic during the same time period. That counter showed traffic was down by 2% in October compared to the previous year, but it’s not clear what could have caused the small drop. It probably didn’t have anything to do with South Coast Rail — early MBTA data for October doesn’t show an increase in train riders compared to the previous month. It’s possible that ramp closures for the [I-195/Route 18 interchange replacement](https://newbedfordlight.org/construction-ramps-up-to-replace-i-195-route-18-interchange/) could have a ripple effect #### **Sept. 5, 1958: The last train to Boston leaves New Bedford**

After about a century of service, the New Haven Railroad [stopped running trains](https://nyti.ms/3O49cl0) to New Bedford, Fall River, and Taunton because of financial losses.

#### **Jan. 24, 1988: The MBTA starts to consider a South Coast commuter rail expansion**

The agency announced tentative plans to extend the Stoughton commuter rail line to Taunton as part of a broader push to expand commuter rail service.

#### **1991: Gov. Bill Weld promises South Coast rail by 1997**

The transportation bond issue the governor [signed](https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/128917188/) in May 1991 funded preliminary environmental and design work to extend the Stoughton line down to New Bedford and Fall River.

“If you don’t have commuter rail by 1997, sue me,” he said at a Fall River Chamber of Commerce meeting that year.

This past Wednesday, just before heading to South Station to catch a commuter train to Readville, Weld told The Light that he remembers saying it — and he doesn’t regret it.

“It was very much our plan,” he said.

#### **August 1996: Transportation bond bill further funds project**

Weld [signed a bill](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/state/1996/08/02/weld-signs-transportation-bill/50631264007/) authorizing $136 million for a commuter rail extension to New Bedford and Fall River.

#### **October 1998: The MBTA starts early construction work**

Even though the exact route had not yet been finalized, Gov. Paul Celucci attended a groundbreaking ceremony in Fall River [kicking off bridge repairs](https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/128921416/) for the South Coast Rail project. Critics at the time called the work premature.

#### **July 16, 2003: Gov. Mitt Romney halts the South Coast Rail project**

The governor [said](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2003/07/17/rail-project-stopped-in-its/50391998007/) the MBTA was years away from any expansions during a visit to Fall River. He cited a lack of funding.

#### **April 4, 2007: Gov. Deval Patrick re-starts the planning process**

The South Coast Rail Plan for Action, [released](https://web.archive.org/web/20110719020048/http://www.eot.state.ma.us/downloads/SCR_plan040407.pdf) by the Patrick administration, renewed the state’s commitment to finishing the project. It put the [price tag](https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/128922270/) at $1.4 billion.

#### **April 17, 2014: The state puts even more money toward South Coast Rail**

As costs continued to rise, the Massachusetts Legislature allocated $2.3 billion for the project.

#### **March 23, 2017: The MBTA settles on a final construction plan**

The plan separated the work into [two phases](https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/128923689/) as a way to complete the project sooner. In the first phase, trains will connect South Coast communities with the Middleborough/Lakeville line by 2024. The second phase will be electric and connect to the Stoughton line in the 2030s.

It was a [controversial move](https://bostonglobe.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/128924662/). State Rep. Bill Straus supported the plan, but Mayor Jon Mitchell was “deeply skeptical.”

#### **July 2, 2019: The MBTA holds another groundbreaking ceremony**

With complete plans for construction and funding — and some construction work already underway — the state held [a ceremony](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2019/07/02/after-nearly-30-years-real/4778348007/) in Freetown to mark the official start of South Coast Rail’s first phase.

#### **Nov. 8, 2022: New Bedford officially joins the MBTA**

Despite some concerns about gentrification, New Bedford voted by an 80% margin to [become an MBTA community](https://newbedfordlight.org/new-bedford-voters-say-yes-to-south-coast-rail/). In Fall River, 78% of voters agreed to join the MBTA.

“I said yes, ‘cause why not?” New Bedford resident Joshua Pound told The Light on Election Day. “I would go to Boston more if it wasn’t for the traffic.”

#### **Late 2023: MBTA officials aim to start running passenger trains**

Construction is expected to finish in September, which will kick off a safety testing process that the agency plans to complete by the end of the year.

[![Image 1: A map at East Taunton station shows the newly extended South Coast Rail routes to Fall River and New Bedford. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)](https://media.wbur.org/wp/2025/03/0314_south-coast-rail-5-2-1920x1220.jpg)](https://media.wbur.org/wp/2025/03/0314_south-coast-rail-5-2.jpg)

A map at East Taunton station shows the newly extended South Coast Rail routes to Fall River and New Bedford. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)

_**Editor's Note:** This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, [sign up here](https://www.wbur.org/news/wburtoday)._

* * *

For the first time in over 65 years, trains from Fall River and New Bedford [rolled into South Station](https://x.com/NewBedfordLight/status/1904116417005265365) this past hour on the opening day of South Coast Rail service. As WBUR’s Andrea Perdomo-Hernandez reports, [roughly 40 years and $1 billion led up to this day](https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/03/21/massachusetts-south-coast-rail-launch-fall-river-new-bedford). And the state is offering [free rides](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march) (!) this week [](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march)— and [every weekend in April](https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/02/27/free-weekends-south-coast-rail-mbta-march) — to get people to try the newly extended commuter rail line.

Whether you’re a traffic-weary commuter or just planning a day trip, here are the basics to know about South Coast Rail:

**Where does it go?** You know the MBTA’s [Middleborough/Lakeville commuter rail line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Middleborough/line)? It’s now called the [Fall River/New Bedford line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/line). South Coast Rail adds five new stations to the line, extending west to Taunton before forking to Freetown and Fall River on one branch and New Bedford on the other. Here’s [a handy map for reference](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/2025-03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map.png).

*   For existing passengers, it’s worth noting: the project also [moved Middleborough’s current stop](https://x.com/MBTA_CR/status/1889358795182047362) closer to the town center.

**How long does it take?** Just over 90 minutes — both from New Bedford and Fall River — to South Station. (Yes, that’s slower than the typical car commute. And no, it doesn’t have Wi-Fi, so maybe bring a book, [listen to a podcast](https://www.wbur.org/podcasts) or use a hotspot if you want to do work.)

**How often does it run?** Weekday trains will run every 70-ish minutes, with more service scheduled around rush hours. Weekend trains will run every two hours. [See the full spring schedule here](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf).

**How much will it cost?** $12.25 for a one-way fare after the current freebies end — or $6 for [those with reduced-fare cards](https://www.mbta.com/fares/reduced). You can also buy a Zone 8 commuter rail pass for $388 a month for unlimited trips.

Psst: Riding on a Saturday or Sunday? Just buy the T’s [$10 commuter rail weekend pass](https://www.mbta.com/fares/commuter-rail-weekends) for unlimited trips each weekend.

**Is there parking**? Yes, all six South Coast Rail stations have lots — and parking will be free through April. After that, rates will be $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends and holidays.

**What’s next?** Technically, this is just the first phase of South Coast Rail. The “[full build](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FullBuild_CorridorMap_2020.pdf)” consists of extending the Stoughton commuter rail line through Raynham to the South Coast — [a more direct route that would be 15 to 25 minutes faster](https://www.wbur.org/news/2022/03/30/mbta-south-coast-rail). But it would also [controversially](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/state/1999/11/21/the-swamp-that-stopped-train/50496452007/) run through protected swampland, among other complications. MBTA officials [have said](https://www.wbur.org/news/2023/10/02/south-coast-rail-opening-timeline-newsletter) it won’t happen until the 2030s at the earliest.

_In other news:_

**Local politicians are paying tribute** to former Massachusetts first lady Kitty Dukakis, who died Friday at the age of 88. Dukakis is remembered as an outspoken advocate for for people living with mental illness and addiction, two issues she was intimately familiar with. She’s survived by her husband, former governor Michael Dukakis, aged 90, and their three children.

*   Worth your time: [Read Dukakis’ full obituary here](https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/03/22/kitty-dukakis-obituary-massachusetts), cowritten by WBUR’s Lynn Jolicoeur and Lisa Mullins.

**Speaking out:** Students from North Andover High School are planning a walkout today at 10 a.m. in protest of staffing cuts across the district. North Andover Public Schools announced last week that it would be [laying off 40 staff members](https://www.wcvb.com/article/north-andover-public-schools-cutting-40-staff-members-next-school-year/64261177) and temporarily shuttering the Kittredge Elementary School to close a $3.5 million budget shortfall in the district’s $68.2 million budget for the coming fiscal year. WBUR’s Cici Yongshi Yu reports the layoffs will affect staff across grade levels.

**Two teenagers were fatally shot** Saturday night outside of Brockton’s Westgate Mall following reports of a fight. Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz [said the victims were “a 15-year-old male and an 18-year-old female,”](https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/03/24/westgate-mall-teen-shooting-brockton-massachusetts) but did not give additional details.

**Sold:** The downtown Boston office tower One Lincoln was auctioned off Friday — [on the literal sidewalk](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/03/21/business/one-lincoln-boston-auction/) — for just $400 million, less than half of its $1 billion valuation three years ago. There was only one bidder: the bank that lent money to the building’s former owner.

P.S. — This Friday, join WBUR reporter Simón Rios at CitySpace for a screening of “Flashpoint: Protests, Policing, and the Press,” an award-winning documentary focusing on the conflict-ridden relationship between police and the press on the frontlines. [Snag your tickets here.](https://www.wbur.org/events/981057/flashpoint-protests-policing-and-the-press-documentary-screening-and-conversation)

The MBTA is tweaking departure times, cutting late-night trains, and changing the route of one peak trip in a new Fall River/New Bedford Line schedule that will take effect on July 21. Departure times for most trips will change by at least a few minutes, and in some cases up to 20 minutes. Many trains will leave earlier on the new schedule. Some afternoon and evening trains will leave slightly later than before. Two late-night [shuttle trains](https://newbedfordlight.org/whats-a-shuttle-train/) will be taken off the weekday schedule. They include a train that left East Taunton at 11:50 p.m. and arrived at New Bedford Station at 12:13 a.m., and another train that left East Taunton at 1:14 a.m. to arrive at Fall River Depot at 1:38 a.m. [The new schedule is online at MBTA.com.](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/2025-07-21-fall-river-new-bedford-line-spring-summer-schedule_0.pdf) A press release from Keolis, the contractor that operates MBTA commuter rail, said the changes were made to improve on-time performance. The announcement said the late-night trains were cut “in order to decrease the number of late-night train movements.” State Sen. Mark Montigny, in his own press release, linked the cuts to [noise complaints](https://newbedfordlight.org/south-coast-residents-speak-up-about-south-coast-rail-noise/) from residents living near the line. The MBTA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updates, which were posted online Wednesday. ### **The MBTA giveth, and the MBTA taketh away** The updated schedule includes a new inbound trip that leaves New Bedford Station at 8:20 a.m. on weekdays, getting to Boston’s South Station at 10 a.m. That fills a gap in the current schedule, which has no departures from New Bedford Station between 7:25 a.m. and 9:33 a.m. But it’s not a net gain for the South Coast region — the MBTA will no longer offer an inbound trip that currently leaves Fall River Depot at 8:22 a.m. on weekdays. Many trips will now skip the JFK/UMass stop, “which will improve travel times for passengers,” according to Keolis. ### **What the late-night cuts mean for riders** For riders trying to get back to New Bedford, the remaining late-night options will include a train leaving South Station at 9:08 p.m. and arriving at New Bedford Station at 10:48 p.m., or a train leaving South Station at 11:59 p.m. and arriving at New Bedford Station at 1:38 a.m. New Bedford-bound riders could take the train leaving South Station at 10:35 p.m., which gets to East Taunton at 11:49 p.m. and arrives in Fall River at 12:14 a.m. But they would need to find their own ride back to New Bedford at the end of the night. SRTA’s last [intercity bus](https://www.srtabus.com/wp-content/uploads/009_FY25_Summer.pdf) leaves Fall River at 9:45 p.m. ![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/IMG_0245.jpeg?resize=780%2C516&ssl=1) South Coast residents voiced concerns at a June 5 meeting about noise and trash near South Coast Rail stations. Credit: Grace Ferguson / The New Bedford Light The MBTA made these changes after a [tense town hall](https://newbedfordlight.org/south-coast-residents-speak-up-about-south-coast-rail-noise/) with South Coast residents in Fall River. Residents said trains were keeping them up late into the night, and MBTA officials promised to take action. South Coast Rail got off to a rocky start after opening on March 24 — staff shortages caused [widespread delays and cancellations](https://newbedfordlight.org/south-coast-rail-disruptions-lead-to-fines-pressure-on-keolis/) during some weekends in April. But Keolis reported this week that trains have operated without staff-related disruptions for the past nine weekends. _Email Grace Ferguson at gferguson@newbedfordlight.org_ _Editor’s note: This story #### [Boston's Morning Newsletter](https://www.wbur.org/tag/wbur-today-newsletter)

![Image 1: A CapeFLYER train arrives in Buzzards Bay during a test run  in May 2013. (Courtesy Wikimedia Commons)](https://wordpress.wbur.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/0520-cape-flyer-wikimediacommons2-1000x750.jpg)

A CapeFLYER train arrives in Buzzards Bay during a test run in May 2013. (Courtesy Wikimedia Commons)

_**Editor's Note:** This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, [sign up here](https://www.wbur.org/news/wburtoday)._

* * *

Summer ain’t over yet. We have three straight days of heat ahead. With the humidity, [the apparent temperature will feel like it’s in the mid-to-upper 90s across much of Massachusetts](https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/1698988574518165630), according to the National Weather Service. Looking for relief? Head to the coast.

Now to the news:

**The seasonal [CapeFLYER train](https://capeflyer.com/) made its final runs of the year** between Boston and Hyannis this weekend. But as the summer tourism season comes to a close, a group of local elected officials are pushing to make passenger train service to Cape Cod a year-round thing. “The CapeFLYER is a tourist train,” says state Rep. Dylan Fernandes, who [filed a bill last week](https://malegislature.gov/Bills/193/HD4555) to bring daily, year-round MBTA commuter rail service to — or at least toward — the Cape. “And we’re for it. We’re supportive of it,” Fernandes told WBUR’s Dave Faneuf. “But we want service that focuses on the 300,000 residents that live here.”

*   Why? Fernandes points to the fact that the Cape’s population [appears to have actually grown over the past couple years](https://provincetownindependent.org/local-journalism-project/next-generation/2023/05/17/as-state-shrinks-cape-cod-has-its-own-odd-crisis/) and that half of its residents commute to the mainland side of the canal. [A 2021 study](https://www.capecodcommission.org/resource-library/file/?url=/dept/commission/team/Website_Resources/transportation/Transit/Cape%20Rail%20Study%20Report.pdf) found that extending commuter rail service to nearby Buzzards Bay would reduce car travel by 10 million to 16 million miles a year.
*   The tracks are already there. But currently, the CapeFLYER only makes a few trips on weekends from Memorial Day to Labor Day. And due to poor track conditions on the Cape, trains are limited to 30 mph once they go over the canal. The $40 roundtrip from South Station to Hyannis takes two and a half hours each way.
*   Fernandes’ bill proposes a two-step approach:

1.  First, it would require the T to extend year-round commuter rail service from the Middleborough/Lakeville line to Buzzards Bay within a year of passage. (This, he says, is a “relatively cheap” near-term solution that avoids issues with the Cape tracks, as well as having to coordinate with the U.S. Army Corps to lower the lift railroad bridge across the Cape Cod Canal.) According to the bill, that means at least three trains in the morning and in the evening on weekdays.
2.  Meanwhile, the bill would require the MBTA to study the feasibility of extending year-round service to Falmouth, Bourne, Barnstable, Yarmouth and Sandwich. That includes the costs and benefits, as well as possible funding sources.

*   Reality check: This isn’t the first time lawmakers have pushed to revive Cape rail. In 2016, a similar pilot proposal was shelved by the MBTA’s oversight board, including the state’s soon-to-be acting transportation secretary, Monica Tibbits-Nutt. “I think there are better things to use our money on,” she [said at the time](https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2016/04/08/mbta-board-not-keen-on-bourne-commuter-rail-plan/). (For now, Fernandes’ bill has just two cosponsors.)
*   Flashback: A century ago, passenger trains used to go all the way to Provincetown. However, the last time the Cape had daily year-round service was 1959. Read [more about the history here](https://capecodcommission.org/resource-library/file?url=%2Fdept%2Fcommission%2Fteam%2FWebsite_Resources%2Ftransportation%2Frtp%2F2-4_Rail_08222011.pdf).

**More classrooms in Boston are now better equipped to take on the heat** as the new school year begins. WBUR’s Carrie Jung [reports that the city has installed thousands of new window air conditioner units](https://www.wbur.org/news/2023/09/05/boston-schools-air-conditioning-installation-heat) across dozens of school buildings as part of Mayor Michelle Wu’s “Green New Deal for Boston Public Schools.”

*   Then and now: Last year, only 20 BPS schools had AC units. Since then, officials have installed more than 3,800 AC units across 78 schools, according to a back-to-school memo released last week. Jung reports there’s another 19 slated to have AC installed, too.
*   Zoom out: NPR [reports](https://www.wbur.org/npr/1196071626/as-classes-resume-in-sweltering-heat-many-schools-lack-air-conditioning) that a lack of air conditioners remains a problem for an estimated 36,000 public schools nationwide.

**Heads up, it’s election day in Massachusetts’ second largest city.** Worcester is holding preliminary elections for its City Council and School Committee races today. There’s a total of five competitive races across the city, including two wide-open City Council contests.

*   Where do I vote? Worcester residents can [enter their address here](https://www.worcesterma.gov/elections/voter-assistance/where-do-i-vote) to find their polling location. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
*   Go deeper: Patch has [more on the candidates here](https://patch.com/massachusetts/worcester/worcester-2023-preliminary-election-voter-guide-council-school-races). The top two vote-getters in each race will advance to the general election.
*   Meanwhile in Worcester: The Boston Globe [reports that longtime Worcester Police Chief Steven Sargent abruptly retired last week](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/09/04/metro/worcester-police-chief-steven-sargent-retires/), amid a federal investigation into the department’s use of force and internal misconduct allegations.

P.S.— Three-time U.S. Poet Laureate Robert Pinsky will be [at CitySpace this Saturday for “Proverbs of Limbo,”](https://www.wbur.org/events/866639/poet-robert-pinsky-presents-proverbs-of-limbo) a combination poetry night and jazz concert. Proceeds from the event will support the next 25 years of the Favorite Poem Project. [Get your tickets here.](https://www.wbur.org/events/866639/poet-robert-pinsky-presents-proverbs-of-limbo)
